title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: By the end of September the timber had been carted in for the cattle yard on the land allotted to the peasants' association, and the butter from the cows had been sold and the profits divided. In practice the system was working splendidly — or at least so it seemed to Levin. To work the subject out theoretically and finish his book — which in Levin's daydreams was not just going to revolutionize political economy but to demolish that science entirely and lay the foundation for a new science of the relationship between the people and the soil — all that was left was to take a tour abroad, study on the spot whatever had been done along the same lines, and gather conclusive evidence that what had been done there was not what was needed. Levin was just waiting on the delivery of his wheat to receive the money for it and set off. But then the rains began, preventing the harvest of the corn and potatoes left in the fields, and putting a stop to all the work, even to the delivery of the wheat.
The mud on the roads was impassable; two mills were carried off, and the weather kept getting worse.

On the 30th of September the sun came out in the morning, and, hoping for fine weather, Levin began making his final preparations to set off. He gave orders for the wheat to be delivered, sent the bailiff to the merchant to collect the money owed him, and went out himself to give a few last directions on the estate before leaving.

Having finished his business, soaked through by the streams of water running down the leather behind his neck and into his gaiters, but in the sharpest and most confident of moods, Levin rode home in the evening. The weather had grown worse than ever toward evening; the hail lashed his drenched mare so hard that she went along sideways, shaking her head and ears; but Levin was fine under his hood, and looked out cheerfully at the muddy streams running under the wheels, at the drops hanging from every bare twig, at the patch of unmelted hailstones still white on the planks of the bridge, at the thick layer of still-juicy, fleshy leaves heaped up around the stripped elm tree. Despite the gloom of nature around him, he felt unusually eager. The conversations he had been having with the peasants in the further village had shown that they were beginning to get used to their new arrangement. The old servant whose hut he had ducked into to dry off plainly approved of Levin's plan and had on his own initiative proposed joining the partnership by buying cattle.

"I only have to keep pushing stubbornly toward my aim, and I'll get there," Levin thought. "And it's something worth working for, worth taking trouble over. This isn't about me individually; the question of the public good comes into it. The whole system of farming — the chief factor in the condition of the people — has to be completely transformed. Instead of poverty, general prosperity and contentment; instead of hostility, harmony and shared interests. In short, a bloodless revolution — but a revolution of the greatest possible scale, starting in our little district, then the province, then Russia, then the whole world. Because a just idea can't help bearing fruit. Yes, this is an aim worth working for. And the fact that it's me — Kostya Levin, who went to a ball in a black tie and got turned down by the Shtcherbatskaya girl, and who, taken as a whole, is such a pitiful, worthless creature — that proves nothing. I'm sure Franklin felt just as worthless about himself, and he too had no faith in himself, taking himself as a whole. That means nothing. And he too probably had an Agafea Mihalovna to whom he confided his secrets."
Mulling over thoughts like these, Levin reached home in the dark.

The bailiff, back from the merchant, had brought part of the money for the wheat. An agreement had been settled with the old servant, and along the way the bailiff had learned that everywhere the corn was still standing in the fields, so that Levin's hundred and sixty shocks still uncarried were nothing compared to other people's losses.

After dinner Levin sat down in his armchair, as he usually did, with a book, and as he read he kept thinking about the journey ahead in connection with his book. Today the whole significance of the book stood out for him with unusual clarity, and whole sections lined themselves up in his mind as illustrations of his theories. "I must write that down," he thought. "That ought to form a brief introduction — which I'd thought unnecessary before." He got up to go to his writing-table, and Laska, lying at his feet, got up too, stretching and looking at him as if to ask which way they were going. But he had no time to write it down, because the head peasants had arrived, and Levin went out into the hall to see them.
After his levee — that is, after giving orders for the next day's work and dealing with all the peasants who had business with him — Levin went back to his study and sat down to work.
Laska lay under the table; Agafea Mihalovna settled into her usual spot with her knitting.
After he had been writing a little while, Levin suddenly thought, with unusual vividness, of Kitty — of her refusal, of their last meeting. He stood up and started pacing the room.
"What's the use of being gloomy?" said Agafea Mihalovna. "Come — why do you stay holed up at home? You ought to go to some warm springs, especially now you're all set for the trip."
"Well, I'm going the day after tomorrow, Agafea Mihalovna; I have to finish my work."

"There, there — your work, you say! As if you hadn't done enough for the peasants! Why, they're already saying, 'Your master is going to get some honor from the Tsar for it.' Funny thing, really — why need you worry yourself over the peasants?"
"I'm not worrying about them; I'm doing it for my own good."

Agafea Mihalovna knew every detail of Levin's plans for his land. Levin often laid out his views to her in their full complexity, and more than once he argued with her and did not agree with her comments. But this time she took what he had said entirely the wrong way.

"The salvation of one's soul is the one thing we all know we must think about before everything else," she said with a sigh. "Now, Parfen Denisitch — for all that he was no scholar — died the kind of death God grant any of us," she said, referring to a servant who had recently passed. "Took the sacrament and all."
"That's not what I mean," he said. "I mean I'm doing it for my own advantage. It's all the better for me if the peasants do their work better."
"Well, whatever you do, if a man's a lazy good-for-nothing, everything will be at sixes and sevens. If he has a conscience, he'll work; if not, there's no doing anything with him."
"Oh, come — you said yourself Ivan has started looking after the cattle better."
"All I say is," Agafea Mihalovna answered, plainly not speaking at random but in strict sequence, "that you ought to get married — that's what I say."

Agafea Mihalovna's pointing at the very subject he had just been thinking about hurt and stung him. Levin scowled, and without answering her sat back down to his work, repeating to himself everything he had been thinking about the real significance of that work. Only now and then he listened in the stillness to the click of Agafea Mihalovna's needles, and, remembering what he didn't want to remember, he frowned again.
At nine o'clock they heard the bell and the faint shake of a carriage coming over the mud.

"Well, here's visitors come to us — now you won't be dull," said Agafea Mihalovna, getting up and heading for the door. But Levin overtook her. His work wasn't going well now, and he was glad of a visitor, whoever it might be.
